prize_parts.citation: for formal and empirical analysis of how constitutions, electoral rules and state capacity shape fiscal policy and economic outcomes

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged on the laureate set. Reading the exchange did not change my view of the merits, but it did sharpen what the citation should claim. The achievement is a unified framework in which political institutions are endogenous and their consequences for policy are testable. Earlier work treated policymakers as benevolent or institutions as given. Persson and Tabellini built the account linking electoral rules and constitutional design to fiscal outcomes and public-goods provision. Besley's work on political agency, accountability and state capacity is a parallel strand that Persson also develops jointly, and that is why I keep the trio. The work is about thirty years old, is in standard graduate training, and has been extended into public economics, development and comparative politics, so I see no timing risk. The chair asked why I regard this as distinct from the 2024 prize. The 2024 prize answered a historical-causal question, whether colonial-era institutions explain long-run differences in prosperity. B045 answers a different one: how specific rules and political incentives shape fiscal and policy choices within a polity. The two are neighbours in subject matter, not the same discovery. I gave the 2024 presentation speech, but speeches for the Academy can reflect collective drafting, and I offer this as my own reading and not as a committee position. In response to the identification critique from Fredriksson, Enflo and Hassler, I would now word the citation around the framework and its testable predictions, not around any single cross-country coefficient. The best-identified evidence in this literature is, to my recollection, the within-country and panel work. The cross-country constitutional regressions are weaker, and I would not let them carry the case.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservations are real and I do not consider them settled. First, the cross-country evidence on constitutions and electoral rules is less credibly identified than the best design-based work on the shortlist, and some results are sensitive to specification. Second, Besley's share is the least separably attributable of the three, and a Persson-Tabellini pair would be the cleaner attribution. I would regard that pair as a defensible fallback, but it fits the constitutions and electoral-rules part of the citation better than the state-capacity part. Third, the Committee may reasonably treat the 2024 prize as close enough to reduce the room for another institutions-themed award, and Acemoglu and Robinson also work in this broad area. Fourth, B037 has the stronger identification and policy reach, and a reasonable member could place it above B045 on scientific grounds. My own discipline sits next to this field, so my confidence in its centrality may be inflated.

responses.point: Hassler moved from B045 as his second choice to B037. He now regards B045 as a riskier lead because of the overlap with the 2024 prize and the weaker causal identification of the cross-country constitutional evidence, and he discounts his own confidence because B045 is near his field.
responses.response: I think his two reasons are the right ones to test, and I accept the identification one largely as stated. It is why I have narrowed my citation to the framework and its predictions. On the 2024 overlap I judge the discoveries distinct, since one is a historical-causal claim about colonial institutions and the other concerns how rules shape fiscal policy within a polity. But I accept that this is a judgement about adjacent fields and that the Committee could weigh the adjacency differently. I would add that his discount for proximity to his own research is the same kind of discount I apply to myself. It means neither of us should lean on field expertise to settle the question. Where we differ is that I do not think weaker cross-country identification outweighs the field-creating character of the work. I also accept that this is a difference in weighting, not a factual disagreement.

responses.point: Enflo ranks B037 first and B045 third. She doubts that B045 is clearly separate from the 2024 prize, because both concern institutions and economic outcomes, and she finds the cross-country constitutional evidence weaker on identification than the micro-designs behind B037. She also defers to my judgement on how distinct the field is.
responses.response: I appreciate the deference and I will try to use it carefully. On substance, the shared theme is real: both prizes concern institutions and outcomes. The difference is in the object of explanation and the type of argument. The 2024 work is a long-run, cross-country causal argument about the origins of institutions. B045 treats institutions as endogenous objects and explains within-polity policy choices through incentives and rules. I concede that B037's design-based evidence is stronger on identification, and I said so in round 1. But identification quality is one criterion among several, and a framework that has organised a whole field and generated testable predictions across public economics, development and comparative politics also counts. I would add that you are right that I am a poor independent judge of whether the Committee will see the fields as separate. I have not claimed that the adjacency risk is zero.

responses.point: Strömberg also ranks B045 first, prefers the trio, but regards Persson and Tabellini alone as the natural fallback if Besley's claim is not separable enough. He proposes limiting the citation to what is distinctive: how electoral rules, constitutions and state capacity shape fiscal and policy outcomes.
responses.response: I agree with the narrow citation and have adopted that logic. I also agree with the fallback, but I want to be precise about what it costs. Persson and Tabellini carry the constitutions and electoral-rules programme most clearly. The state-capacity and accountability strand is where Besley's contribution lies, and it is linked to Persson through joint work. A pair prize would therefore drop one half of my citation and I would have to rewrite it, not just remove a name. That is why I keep the trio as my single proposal while treating the pair as acceptable. I do not think the Committee should include Besley merely to broaden the award, so if members who know the attribution better judge his strand not separable, I would accept the pair and narrow the wording.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee reads B045 as sufficiently distinct from the 2024 institutions prize, given that I gave that speech and may be biased toward seeing a distinction.
Whether Besley's state-capacity and accountability strand is separable enough for a trio, or whether Persson and Tabellini alone would be the sharper attribution.
How much the weaker causal identification of the cross-country constitutional evidence should count against a field whose strength is its framework and testable predictions.

Whether B037 should be judged one coherent discovery. If so, I regard it as scientifically stronger on identification, and my reservation about it would then be limited to the Katz-versus-Dorn attribution.

My judgements about B037, B025 and the other non-political-economy candidates are those of a political scientist and rely on my reading of colleagues' arguments. I have not independently verified any sources.
statement.conflict_note: Update in response to the chair's request. In round 1 I referred to a Stockholm connection that I attributed to Hassler's opening. It does not appear in his round-1 file, so I cannot identify which candidate it concerned and I withdraw it as unsupported. What I can disclose is this. I am a Stockholm University professor in the Department of Political Science, and committee members Hassler, Krusell and Boppart are at IIES in the same university but a different department. To my recollection, which is not in my supplied profile and which I have not verified, Torsten Persson is also affiliated with Stockholm University (IIES). If so, one name in my preferred configuration is a university colleague, though not in my department. My profile lists no collaboration with Persson, Tabellini or Besley, and my long-time collaborators (Rothstein, Lapuente, Hadenius, Dahlström, Holmberg, Bäck and Lindvall) are not on any shortlisted ballot. My field (comparative politics, democratisation and quality of government) is adjacent to B045. I know of no further conflict among members beyond those already filed. All of this is disclosed and not adjudicated.
